stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
Trees in cooler climates tend to have leaves with toothed rather than smooth edges, so paleobotanists often estimate past temperatures from the percentage of toothed-margin species in a fossil flora. Paleobotanist Ines Haldane cautions that the method can mislead. Plants along streams root in wet, frequently disturbed soils; such soils favor fast-growing species; and fast-growing species are disproportionately toothed. A streamside setting, Haldane argues, can therefore raise a flora's toothed percentage even when temperature does not differ. For example, ______

Four Fossil Floras
Flora | Setting | Temperature from isotope data (°C) | Toothed-margin species (%)
P | Streamside | 18 | 41
Q | Upland lake | 18 | 27
R | Streamside | 14 | 55
S | Upland lake | 14 | 38
choices: Flora P (streamside, 18°C) had a higher percentage of toothed-margin species than Flora Q (upland lake, 18°C) did.
Flora R (streamside, 14°C) had a higher percentage of toothed-margin species than Flora Q (upland lake, 18°C) did.
Flora S (upland lake, 14°C) had a higher percentage of toothed-margin species than Flora Q (upland lake, 18°C) did.
Flora S (upland lake, 14°C) had a higher percentage of toothed-margin species than Flora R (streamside, 14°C) did.
explanation: Work out what the example has to show before you read the choices. Haldane's claim has a scope phrase: a streamside setting raises the toothed percentage 'even when temperature does not differ.' So the example has to compare a streamside flora with a non-streamside flora at the same temperature, and the streamside flora has to have the higher percentage. Floras P and Q were both 18°C, P is streamside, and P has 41% against Q's 27%. Setting is the only thing that differs between them, so the difference can be put down to setting.

B.why: This is the second-order trap. You saw correctly that the example needs streamside versus non-streamside, and R (55%) is higher than Q (27%). But R is also 4°C cooler than Q, and cooler climates have more toothed species anyway. The gap could come entirely from temperature, so it doesn't show what setting does when temperature is held equal.

C.why: This reading is accurate: S (38%) is higher than Q (27%). But both floras come from upland lakes. The only difference is temperature, so this shows the familiar temperature effect, not Haldane's point about streamside settings. You picked a true comparison that doesn't prove the passage's claim.

D.why: You picked the right kind of pair (same temperature, different setting) but got the direction backwards. At 14°C, streamside Flora R has 55% and upland-lake Flora S has 38%, so S is lower than R. The choice misreads the table, and the comparison it states would actually count against Haldane's claim.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the example?
stimulus: City planners often widen sidewalks by narrowing traffic lanes, expecting the added room to draw more pedestrians. In hot months, however, unshaded concrete absorbs heat, and hot pavement discourages walking, so extra sidewalk space may attract few people unless something keeps it cool. After studying 40 downtown blocks from 2023 to 2025, urban planner Tomás Reyes-Whitfield concluded that widening sidewalks increased summer afternoon foot traffic only on blocks where street trees shaded the sidewalk. For example, ______

figure.caption: Change in Summer Afternoon Foot Traffic on 40 Downtown Blocks, 2023–2025
figure.alt: Bar graph of the percent change in summer afternoon pedestrian counts for four block types: widened and shaded, unwidened and shaded, widened and unshaded, and unwidened and unshaded. The vertical axis runs from 0 to 28 percent in steps of 4.

choices: widened, shaded blocks gained 24%, versus 8% for unwidened, shaded blocks, while widened and unwidened unshaded blocks each gained 4%.
widened, shaded blocks gained 24%, versus 4% for widened, unshaded blocks, while unwidened, shaded blocks gained just 8%.
widened, shaded blocks gained 24%, versus 4% for unwidened, unshaded blocks, while unwidened, shaded blocks gained just 8%.
widened, shaded blocks gained 24%, versus 8% for unwidened, shaded blocks, while widened, unshaded blocks gained more than unwidened ones.
explanation: The word 'only' means the example has to show two things. First, among shaded blocks, widening raised foot traffic: widened blocks gained 24% and unwidened blocks gained 8%. Second, among unshaded blocks, widening made no difference: widened and unwidened blocks both gained 4%. Choice A is the only option that states both comparisons, each with shade held constant. Together they show that widening helped where there was shade and did not help where there wasn't.

B.why: These numbers are read correctly, but the main comparison (24% versus 4%) is between two widened blocks that differ in shade. That shows shade matters once a sidewalk is widened. It doesn't show what widening does on unshaded blocks, because there's no unwidened, unshaded baseline. The 4% could still be a gain caused by widening, so 'only on shaded blocks' isn't established.

C.why: Comparing widened, shaded blocks (24%) with unwidened, unshaded blocks (4%) changes two things at once. The gap could come from widening, from shade, or from both, so it can't show that widening works only where there is shade. You went with the biggest gap on the graph instead of a comparison that isolates widening.

D.why: This choice starts with the right comparison, which is why it's tempting once you've found the key idea. But it finishes by misreading the graph: widened and unwidened unshaded blocks both gained 4%, so neither gained more. And if widening had helped unshaded blocks, that would undercut the word 'only' in the claim rather than support it.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
Low-frequency traffic noise can mask birdsong, and birds in noisy places often sing with a higher minimum frequency. Because cities are noisy, it is hard to tell whether this shift responds to noise itself or to other features of urban life. After recording great tits at four sites, a research team concluded that traffic noise outweighed setting, urban or rural, in predicting a site's minimum song frequency. For example, ______

Minimum Song Frequency of Great Tits at Four Sites
Site | Setting | Traffic noise (dB) | Minimum frequency (kHz)
P | Urban | 68 | 3.4
Q | Urban | 49 | 2.6
R | Rural | 67 | 3.3
S | Rural | 47 | 2.5
choices: urban site P had a higher minimum frequency than rural site S.
rural site R had a higher minimum frequency than rural site S.
rural site R had a higher minimum frequency than urban site Q.
urban site Q had a higher minimum frequency than rural site R.
explanation: To show that noise outweighs setting, you need a case where the two pull in opposite directions. Site R is rural but noisy (67 dB), and site Q is urban but quiet (49 dB). R's higher minimum frequency (3.3 kHz against 2.6 kHz) means noise won even though the setting pointed the other way.

A.why: This is true, but P is both urban and noisy while S is both rural and quiet. Either factor could explain the gap, so it can't show that one outweighs the other.

B.why: You saw that you needed to separate noise from setting, and this does show that noise matters when setting is held constant. But the claim is that noise outweighs setting, and only a comparison that sets the two against each other can show that.

D.why: You reversed the data. Q's minimum frequency is 2.6 kHz, which is lower than R's 3.3 kHz.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
stimulus:
Soluble fibers such as beta-glucan thicken the contents of the small intestine, and that added viscosity slows the rate at which glucose passes into the blood. A nutrition team therefore argued that what blunts the rise in blood glucose after a meal is the viscosity a fiber creates, not simply the amount of fiber a food contains. As evidence, the team noted that ______

Blood Glucose After Eating Four Test Breads
Bread | Added fiber | Intestinal viscosity (mPa·s) | Peak glucose rise (mmol/L)
W | None | 5 | 3.2
X | 6 g cellulose | 6 | 3.1
Y | 3 g beta-glucan | 240 | 2.0
Z | 6 g beta-glucan | 410 | 1.4
choices: bread Z, which contained 6 grams of added fiber, produced a smaller glucose rise than bread W, which contained none.
bread Y, which contained 3 grams of added fiber, produced a smaller glucose rise than bread X, which contained 6 grams.
bread Z, which contained 6 grams of added fiber, produced a smaller glucose rise than bread Y, which contained 3 grams.
bread X, which contained 6 grams of added fiber, produced a smaller glucose rise than bread Y, which contained 3 grams.
explanation: To show it is viscosity rather than amount, you need a bread with less fiber but more viscosity that still does better. Bread Y has half the fiber of bread X but far more viscosity (240 against 6), and it produced the smaller rise (2.0 against 3.1). That beats an explanation based on amount alone.

A.why: This is accurate, but Z has both more fiber and more viscosity than W. The result fits the 'amount of fiber' explanation just as well, so it can't single out viscosity.

C.why: You may have noticed that Z is more viscous than Y. But Z also has more fiber, so this looks like an ordinary dose effect and doesn't rule out the amount explanation the team rejects.

D.why: This misreads the table. Bread X produced a rise of 3.1 mmol/L, which is larger than bread Y's 2.0, not smaller.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
Fly ash, a by-product of burning coal, can replace part of the cement in concrete. It reacts slowly, gradually filling pores that would otherwise let chloride from road salt seep in and corrode steel reinforcement; lower penetration values indicate better resistance. Because of that slow reaction, engineers testing bridge-deck mixes argued that the standard 28-day test understates the advantage fly ash gives over plain concrete. For example, ______

Chloride Penetration of Concrete Samples (coulombs)
Curing time | Plain mix | 25% fly ash mix
28 days | 3,300 | 3,150
90 days | 2,900 | 1,250
choices: the fly ash mix allowed 1,900 fewer coulombs through at 90 days than it had allowed at 28 days.
the plain mix improved by more between 28 and 90 days than the fly ash mix improved.
at 90 days, the fly ash mix allowed 1,650 fewer coulombs through than the plain mix did.
the fly ash mix's advantage over the plain mix grew from 150 coulombs to 1,650 coulombs.
explanation: The claim is about the advantage over plain concrete, which is a gap between the two mixes, and about how that gap looks at 28 days compared with later. At 28 days the gap is only 150 coulombs (3,300 − 3,150). By 90 days it is 1,650 (2,900 − 1,250). A 28-day test would therefore have badly understated it.

A.why: This is true, but the plain mix also improved over time. Tracking one mix alone says nothing about its advantage over the other.

B.why: This has it backwards. The plain mix improved by 400 coulombs, and the fly ash mix improved by 1,900.

C.why: You correctly treated the advantage as a gap between the mixes, but this gives only the 90-day gap. To show the 28-day test understates the advantage, you also need the much smaller gap at 28 days.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
In woodblock printing, each pass of the press slightly crushes the raised wood, and the thin ridges that carry fine lines crush fastest. Hard fruitwoods such as cherry and pear have long been preferred, but they are costly. One printmaker argues that basswood, a cheaper soft wood, is a sound substitute for blocks carved only with broad areas of color, even if it is a poor choice for fine-line work. For example, ______

Impressions Printed Before Visible Block Wear
Wood | Fine-line areas | Broad color areas
Cherry | 900 | 2,400
Pear | 850 | 2,500
Basswood | 300 | 2,350
Pine | 250 | 1,100
choices: basswood lasted nearly as many impressions as cherry in broad areas but only a third as many in fine-line areas.
basswood lasted roughly eight times as many impressions in broad areas as it did in fine-line areas.
pine, like basswood, lasted no more than a third as many impressions as cherry in fine-line areas.
basswood lasted more impressions than pear in broad areas but fewer than pear in fine-line areas.
explanation: The claim has two parts, and both compare basswood with the hardwoods it would replace. In broad areas basswood nearly matches cherry (2,350 against 2,400), so it is a sound substitute there. In fine lines it manages only a third as many impressions (300 against 900), so it is a poor choice for that work.

B.why: This is true, but every wood lasts far longer in broad areas than in fine-line areas. Comparing basswood only with itself can't show it measures up to the hardwoods it would replace.

C.why: This is accurate, but it supports only the fine-line half of the claim, and it brings in pine, which the printmaker isn't recommending.

D.why: This misreads the broad-area column. Basswood's 2,350 impressions is fewer than pear's 2,500, not more.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the example?
stimulus: Bleaching occurs when heat- or light-stressed corals expel the algae that live in their tissues. In a tank experiment, researchers kept coral fragments at either normal (28°C) or heat-wave (31°C) temperature, under either full light or shade cloth. They concluded that shading is worth deploying on reefs only during heat waves, since in water of normal temperature it makes little difference. For example, ______

figure.caption: Coral Fragments Bleached After Four Weeks
figure.alt: Bar graph of the percentage of coral fragments bleached under four conditions: 28°C unshaded, 28°C shaded, 31°C unshaded and 31°C shaded.

choices: at 31°C, shaded fragments bleached at a rate 36 percentage points lower than unshaded ones did.
shading lowered bleaching by 36 percentage points at 31°C but by only 4 points at 28°C.
at 28°C, shaded fragments bleached at a rate only 4 percentage points lower than unshaded ones did.
unshaded fragments bleached at a rate 44 percentage points higher at 31°C than at 28°C.
explanation: The conclusion makes two claims: shading helps a lot in a heat wave, and it barely helps at normal temperature. Only this choice gives both. Shading lowered bleaching from 56% to 20% at 31°C, a drop of 36 points, but only from 12% to 8% at 28°C, a drop of 4 points.

A.why: This is accurate, but it covers only the heat-wave half. It doesn't show that shading makes little difference in water of normal temperature, which is the reason the researchers give.

C.why: This is accurate and matches the clause after 'since', but on its own it doesn't show that shading is worth using during heat waves. You stopped after supporting one half of the claim.

D.why: This is true, but it measures the effect of heat on unshaded corals. The conclusion is about what shading does, and this choice never compares shaded with unshaded fragments.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
Wolves are thought to help beavers indirectly. By keeping elk on the move, wolves reduce browsing on streamside willows, and beavers depend on tall willows for food and building material. Some ecologists claim, however, that wolves alone are not enough: in valleys where willows have stayed short, the presence of wolves has done nothing for beavers. For example, ______

Wolves, Willows, and Beavers in Four Valleys
Valley | Wolves present | Average willow height (m) | Beaver colonies
1 | Yes | 3.1 | 7
2 | Yes | 1.0 | 1
3 | No | 2.9 | 6
4 | No | 0.9 | 1
choices: Valley 1, which has wolves, supports more beaver colonies than Valley 4, which does not.
Valley 3, which lacks wolves, supports nearly as many beaver colonies as Valley 1, which has them.
Valley 2, which has wolves, supports no more beaver colonies than Valley 4, which does not.
Valley 2, which has wolves, supports more beaver colonies than Valley 3, which does not.
explanation: The claim is limited to valleys where willows stayed short, and it says wolves made no difference there. Valleys 2 and 4 both have short willows (1.0 m and 0.9 m). Valley 2 has wolves and Valley 4 doesn't, yet each has just one colony.

A.why: This is true, but the two valleys differ in both wolves and willow height, and Valley 1's willows are tall. It looks like wolves helping, which is the opposite of the point being made.

B.why: You rightly saw that the willows matter more than the wolves. But this compares two tall-willow valleys and shows that beavers can do without wolves. The claim is about short-willow valleys, where wolves don't help.

D.why: This misreads the table. Valley 2 has 1 colony and Valley 3 has 6.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
Economists often express the union wage premium, meaning how much more union members earn than comparable nonmembers, in relative terms, since a $3 raise means more to a worker earning $10 an hour than to one earning $40. Analyzing hourly wages by education level, one economist claims that, measured this way, union membership benefits the least-educated workers most. For example, ______

Median Hourly Wage by Education and Union Membership
Education | Union members | Nonmembers
No diploma | $18 | $12
High school diploma | $28 | $20
Bachelor's degree | $40 | $36
choices: union members with a high school diploma out-earned nonmembers by $8 an hour, the largest dollar gap of any group.
union members with a bachelor's degree earned $40 an hour, the highest wage of any group in the table.
union members with a high school diploma earned 40% more than nonmembers did, the largest relative gap of any group.
union members without a diploma earned 50% more than nonmembers did, the largest relative gap of any group.
explanation: The phrase 'measured this way' means the premium has to be relative. For workers without a diploma, $18 is 50% more than $12. That beats 40% for high school graduates ($28 against $20) and about 11% for bachelor's degree holders ($40 against $36), so the least-educated group benefits most.

A.why: The $8 figure is correct, but it is a dollar gap. The economist measures the premium in relative terms, and on that measure this group comes second.

B.why: This is true, but it gives a single wage rather than a premium. It never compares members with nonmembers, so it doesn't address the claim.

C.why: You calculated 40% correctly for high school graduates but didn't check the other rows. Workers without a diploma have a larger relative gap, at 50%.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
stimulus:
Some self-healing plastics contain tiny capsules of liquid resin that burst when a crack forms and fill the gap. Heat can also close cracks on its own, by letting polymer chains flow. A team that tested otherwise identical samples with and without capsules cautioned that their headline result, 75 percent strength recovery at 60°C, overstates what the capsules themselves achieve, since ______

Strength Recovered After Healing (%)
Healing temperature | With capsules | Without capsules
20°C | 35 | 5
60°C | 75 | 40
choices: samples without capsules recovered 40 percent of their strength when healed at 60°C.
samples with capsules recovered 75 percent of their strength at 60°C, the highest figure in the table.
at 60°C, samples with capsules recovered more strength than samples without capsules did.
at 60°C, samples without capsules recovered more strength than samples with capsules did.
explanation: To show that 75% overstates what the capsules do, you need the share of that recovery that would happen without them. Capsule-free samples at the same temperature recovered 40% from heat alone, so the capsules account for only about 35 of the 75 points.

B.why: This only restates the headline figure. It gives no baseline to compare it with, so it can't show that the figure overstates anything.

C.why: This is true, but it shows the capsules helping, which is the opposite of the team's warning. You picked a correct reading that points the wrong way.

D.why: This reverses the 60°C row. Samples without capsules recovered 40%, which is less than the 75% recovered by samples with capsules.
